content: Cayston (aztreonam inhalation) is prescribed to improve respiratory symptoms in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) who are infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The recommended dosage is 75 mg inhaled every 8 hours for 28 days. It must be administered using the Altera nebulizer system, and treatment should not be repeated for another 28 days after completing a course. Doses should be spaced at least 4 hours apart. Before administering Cayston, a bronchodilator should be used. Short-acting beta-agonists should be taken 15 minutes to 4 hours prior, while long-acting beta-agonists should be taken 30 minutes to 12 hours before. If mucolytics are part of the treatment regimen, they should be taken after bronchodilators but before aztreonam. The vials and diluent should be stored refrigerated at 2–8°C (36–46°F). Once removed from refrigeration, they can be stored at room temperature (up to 25°C or 77°F) for up to 28 days. The medication should be used immediately after reconstitution, and only one dose should be reconstituted at a time. Cayston is not recommended for patients under 7 years of age, as safety and efficacy have not been established in this population. For patients aged 7 years and older, the dosing is the same as for adults: 75 mg inhaled every 8 hours for 28 days, using the Altera nebulizer, with a 28-day break before repeating treatment. Adverse effects reported include cough (54%), nasal congestion (16%), wheezing (16%), pharyngolaryngeal pain (12%), fever (13%), chest discomfort (8%), abdominal pain (7%), vomiting (6%), bronchospasm (3%), and rash (2%). Hypersensitivity and allergic reactions have been observed in clinical trials. If an allergic reaction occurs, treatment should be discontinued. Bronchospasm may also occur; if chest tightness develops during nebulizer use, treatment should be stopped. Cayston has been shown to increase FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) during the 28-day treatment course. Baseline FEV1 should be considered when evaluating post-treatment changes, as these may be due to pulmonary exacerbations. There is an increased risk of drug-resistant bacteria in the absence of known Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection. Data on the use of Cayston in pregnant women is insufficient to determine the risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. However, systemic absorption of aztreonam following inhalation is expected to be minimal. Cystic fibrosis during pregnancy may increase the risk of preterm delivery. Following intravenous administration, aztreonam is excreted in human milk at concentrations less than 1% of maternal serum levels. Peak plasma concentrations of aztreonam after a 75 mg inhaled dose are approximately 1% of those observed following a 500 mg IV dose. Systemic absorption after inhalation is minimal, and there is no data on the effects of the drug on breastfed infants or milk production. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for therapy and any potential adverse effects on the infant from the drug or the underlying maternal condition. Pharmacokinetics of aztreonam include a peak plasma time of approximately 1 hour, with 56% protein binding. The drug is primarily excreted via urine (60–70%) and feces (13–15%). Mean sputum concentrations after a single dose are 726 mcg/g, and after multiple doses on days 1, 14, and 28, they are 984 mcg/g, 793 mcg/g, and 715 mcg/g, respectively. This information is provided for general educational purposes and may vary depending on individual circumstances. Always consult the applicable healthcare provider or plan for the most current and specific information.
